title: Pump Station
passages:
The pedal-rail’s rear bearing screamed and let go. Kass felt it in her teeth before she heard it, a whine climbing into a screech, and then smoke, black and greasy, curled up from the housing behind her left heel. She threw her weight off the crossbar before the wheel could lock and pitch her into the alkali dust. She coasted the last half mile into Culvert Nine on dead legs, the rail humming up through her frame, her lungs full of burnt copper and fine gray grit.

Her thighs were cramping hard enough to make her knees shake. She had ridden PR-ANZA-03 out of Anza’s shed chalked live to Culvert Nine, pedaling after Miko and the blank rig while the shift bell counted down toward 18:00. Twenty minutes left, maybe less, and her body was already bargaining to stop.

The station resolved out of the haze: a dead pump house squatting beside dry intake pipes the width of her torso, a rusted settling tank listing into the scrub, and the receiving jaw sitting shut between them. It was a hydraulic clamp-and-weigh throat built to match a canister’s seal stamp against a manifest before it would unclamp the storeroom door. Kass had seen loaders lose fingers to jaws that closed early, and she had no intention of becoming a cautionary tale at a pencil-marked station she had never visited.

On the ridge above the switch, the blank rig sat stopped. No plates, no board, no transponder squawk. Its hand lamp still burned in the crew box window, a single yellow light in the alkali haze, and no one was climbing down.

Kass eased her boot to the rail and stood up slowly. Her hands were numb from gripping the crossbar. “Miko,” she said to the empty station. “You better not be dead up there.”

The rig did not answer. The lamp did not flicker. It just waited, burning, while eleven warm canisters rode the deck with no name on the plates.

A shadow moved behind the rig’s windshield. Not a trick of the light. Something shifted in the glass, dark against the yellow glow, then settled back. Kass froze. Whoever was in the crew box was still breathing, still alive, and not coming down.

The pump house door banged open against the wind. A figure stepped out onto the cracked concrete apron, one hand on a hand-cranked work lamp mounted on a tripod, the other holding a clipboard that had seen more alkali dust than paper. They wore a grease-stained canvas coat with the sleeves rolled to the elbows, and their beard was gray at the chin, black at the jaw. They didn't walk — they planted each boot like they owned the ground under it.

They set the tripod down with a thud, braced a knee against the leg, and started cranking. The flywheel whined, the reflector spun up, and a hard white circle cut through the haze. It hit Kass square in the chest, pinning her to the rail like a specimen.

"Thief," they said. Their voice carried over the wind without strain. "Don't move. Don't reach. Don't speak until I say."

Kass's hands stayed on the crossbar. Her badge was in her chest pocket, the chain warm against her sternum. "I'm not — "

"Outsiders get chalked once under the station name," they said, reading from the clipboard like it was scripture. "One mark. One name. One chance to prove you're not here to take. You get nothing until the storeroom agrees. There is no third mark. There is no appeal. There is no 'but I'm from Anza.'"

They flipped a page. The wind tore at the edges. The blank rig's lamp burned steady on the ridge above. Inside, the shadow behind the windshield hadn't moved.

Kass's fingers closed on the badge in her chest pocket before her brain caught up. She pulled it out, the metal warm from her skin, and held it up into the white circle. "K-774. Anza dispatcher. Chain live as of oh-eight-hundred. Teodoro signed it himself."

Saul didn't flinch. Didn't even blink. The crank handle kept turning in their other hand, flywheel humming, the light steady as a surgeon's lamp. They looked at the badge the way a cat looks at a moth beating against a screen.

"Paper doesn't pump," they said. "A badge from a live node is worth exactly nothing at a pencil mark. You know how many live nodes have gone dark since winter started? I've got a clipboard full of names that were live at breakfast and buried by lunch. Your chain means you got a meal ticket at Anza. It don't mean shit here."

Kass's jaw tightened. Her legs screamed. The bearing housing behind her heel was still radiating heat through her boot sole. "I'm not asking for a meal. I'm telling you eleven canisters on that rig are Anza's payment, struck full at our own jaw. Nour signed the tally. Doan witnessed. That rig rolled out of Anza's ore stub two hours ago."

"Anza's ore stub," Saul repeated, flat. "The one with the red trust score. The one where the overlap key died and the clearance got pulled. The one where a blank rig just *happened* to show up with eleven warm cans and no plates." They flipped the clipboard page again, scribbled something with a carpenter's pencil. "You want to tell me how a dispatcher ends up chasing a ghost rig on a pedal-rail with a seized bearing? That's not a schedule. That's a story."

"It's the truth."

"Truth's a luxury. We deal in weight." Saul set the pencil behind their ear. "Chalk your name. One mark. Station name. Then we see what the storeroom says."

Kass's throat worked. She looked at the ridge. The blank rig's lamp burned steady. The shadow behind the windshield hadn't moved. Miko was up there — had to be — and the canisters were ticking down toward cold-cycle lockout. Every minute she spent arguing was a minute the jaw stayed shut.

She reached into her other pocket. Her fingers found the folded ticket, the graphite thumbprint smudged against the cheap cardstock. She pulled it out and held it up. "This was in the dust at Anza's stub. J. Renner. Bought name. Miko dropped it running for that rig. Doan saw her swing into the crew box. She's *on* that rig, Saul. She's not a thief. She's one of ours."

Saul leaned forward. The light caught the gray in their beard, the lines around their eyes. They took the ticket between two fingers, turned it over, held it up to the beam. The graphite thumbprint caught the light, dull and definite.

"J. Renner," they read. "Coast passage. Bought name. Graphite print." They looked at Kass. "The name on it isn't yours. The print *is* yours. Or close enough that the desk won't ask questions." They folded the ticket slow, deliberate. "That's not proof she's yours, dispatcher. That's proof *you* handled stolen paper. At a pencil mark, that makes you the thief."

Kass's hands curled on the crossbar. "I didn't steal it. I *found* it."

"Found it in the dust where a runner dropped it running for an unplated rig." Saul tucked the ticket into their coat pocket. "That's the story the storeroom hears. You want to change the story, you put something on the plate the storeroom can weigh. A badge don't weigh nothing. A ticket don't weigh nothing. Your word don't weigh nothing."

The wind gusted, rattling the pump house door on its hinges. Somewhere in the station's guts, a valve hissed. The blank rig's lamp didn't waver.

"Chalk," Saul said. "Name. Station. One mark. Then you wait."

The storeroom ramp was a slot of dark cut into the settling tank's flank, and something came up it unhurried, one boot at a time, the way people climb when they've learned that hurrying is how you get robbed.

She was shorter than Saul and built like the pump house, a canvas apron over a coat, a tally slate under one arm with a carpenter's pencil shoved through the twine. In her other fist, a wedge of bread. She took a bite of it, chewed, and looked at Kass the way a buyer looks at a boot.

"Saul. Off the crank. You're wasting my flywheel."

Saul eased the handle. The white circle shrank to a hard coin on Kass's sternum and stayed there.

The woman came out to the edge of the apron, stopped where the concrete gave over to dust, and held out her free hand. Saul gave her the ticket. She turned it over twice, read the name, rubbed the graphite thumbprint with her thumb, and handed it back.

Then she looked down at Kass's boots. Really looked, at the split welt and the alkali crust to the ankle.

"Node boots," she said. "Anza boots. You rode that thing yourself, then. All the way up the ore line on a dead bearing." She bit the bread again. "That's not a thief's work. Thieves ride."

"I'm a dispatcher."

"You're a person with a badge, which out here is a different animal." Brill's chin lifted toward the ridge, where the blank rig sat with its lamp burning. "And that's a rig with no plates sitting in my switch light, and somebody in the box who hasn't come down. So before you tell me another word about Anza, you're going to hear how my jaw works, because you've clearly got a plan that involves it."

She jerked the pencil out of the twine and pointed it at the throat. The clamp-and-weigh sat squat between the intake pipes, four hydraulic rams holding a steel mouth shut, the reader plate on its left cheek dark as a closed eye.

"That reads a seal stamp. It matches it to a manifest and it opens, and the cans go in, and the door shuts, and everybody eats. Now. Every canister on this line is sealed under a receiving mark. Break that seal at my throat — pop one to see what's inside, tap one for a taste, doesn't matter, doesn't matter if you put the lid back on — the throat calls it an unsealed vessel and faults. Clamp pins. Whole run locks. Not just mine. The ore spur too."

"So call Kettering."

"Kettering's nearest reader's six weeks up the line, and Kettering stopped caring somewhere in the second week." She said it without heat, the way you'd read a gauge. "So we'd sit locked till spring, and I'd be watching the people behind that door get thin while I explained the rule to them. I don't skim. Not for you. Not for my own crew. Not for a badge with a live chain on it, and not with a lamp burning up on my ridge like an invitation."

She folded her arms, bread still in her fist.

"That's the whole of it. Weight in, weight out, seals whole. Everything else a person brings me — promises, manifests, chain scores, a story about a red node and a dead overlap key — I've been handed all of it before, by people who were gone by the second bell. A full storeroom I can count. You I can't."

Behind her, deep under the tank, something metal shifted and settled. Then a cough, muffled, and another one answering it further back. Brill didn't turn around.

"You hear that? That's not machinery."

Kass's legs were shaking openly now. "Then let me show you the reader. Eleven cans, struck full at Anza's own jaw. You put them through clean, nothing gets opened, nothing faults."

"Nothing gets opened," Brill repeated. "You just told me what you want, and what you want is my throat open on plates nobody claims." She put the last of the bread in her mouth. "Also, they're going cold, dispatcher. Cans that sit warm too long past their run start their lockout, and once they lock, a clean manifest won't save you either."

She wiped her hands on the apron and looked up the grade at the rig, at the yellow square of the crew box window.

"Six minutes now," she said. "Whoever's up there has been sitting in my light six minutes, waiting to be told what she's worth. That's smarter than you."
